SonoHL is an investigational device. It has not been cleared or approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, is not available for sale, and is limited by federal law to investigational use. Statements on this site describe development objectives and hypotheses, not demonstrated performance or approved intended uses.
Investigational Acoustic-Sensing Platform

Toward Multi-Point Heart and Lung Sound Capture

SonoHL is developing a wearable platform intended to capture heart sounds — with lung-sound capture under separate evaluation — from multiple predetermined positions, and to organize those recordings for review by a qualified reviewer. The exact product configuration, intended use, clinical output, and regulatory pathway remain under development. The platform is investigational and is not available for commercial sale.

The Problem

Acoustic examination depends on acquisition and interpretation.

Examiner experience, placement consistency, recording conditions, ambient noise, and access to specialist review can vary across care settings. These factors support investigation of more standardized acoustic capture and shareable recordings.

Acquisition Interpretation Workflow Remote feasibility
Development considerations Acoustic capture and review can vary across settings.
Acquisition consistencyPlacement and recording conditions can affect the signals collected.
Interpretation accessSome settings may have limited access to cardiopulmonary expertise.
Workflow burdenTesting, consultation, travel, and follow-up may create operational burdens.
Remote-care feasibilityRemote use requires validated setup, transmission, privacy, review, and escalation workflows.
Development hypothesis SonoHL is investigating whether consistent multi-point recordings can be stored, shared, compared, and reviewed by clinicians.
Proposed Development Uses

Acoustic assessment and remote review concepts.

These proposed workflows are development hypotheses. They are not approved intended uses, cleared indications, commercial claims, or confirmed remote-monitoring services.

In-person concept

Point-of-care acoustic assessment support

In a proposed workflow, an intended user would apply the vest, obtain recordings under a defined protocol, confirm recording quality, and make the acoustic information available for review by a qualified reviewer.

Apply under a defined protocol Confirm recording quality Present information for human review
Future evaluation

Repeat recording and remote review

The platform may be evaluated for repeat recording in supervised home, clinic, rural-health, or nursing-station settings. Remote use is not represented as ready or validated.

Validate operator training and fit Establish secure data transfer Define review and escalation workflows
Platform Concept

A wearable concept for organized acoustic capture and review.

SonoHL is developing a sensor vest, supporting software, and a clinician-facing review environment for acquiring heart and lung sounds from predetermined positions and organizing recordings for human review.

Acquisition concept

Predetermined sensor positions

The vest concept positions acoustic sensors across multiple areas of the chest and back. Repeatability and placement tolerance require formal verification and human-factors validation.

Review concept

Organized recordings

The proposed software environment would store and organize recordings and associated information for review by a qualified reviewer.

Future research

Shareable acoustic information

Repeat recordings and remote sharing may be evaluated as future workflows after setup, transmission, privacy, cybersecurity, review, and escalation processes are validated.

Being developed as a clinician-support platform.

SonoHL is not represented as replacing medical judgment, independently diagnosing disease, or establishing treatment decisions. Its first intended use and clinical output have not yet been approved.

Investigational Human review Evidence development
Technology

Capture, quality control, processing, and review.

The development workflow is to acquire time-stamped acoustic signals from the active sensor configuration, apply defined quality checks and processing steps, and present recordings and associated information for human review.

Core system

A vest-based acoustic-sensing platform in development.

The system concept combines wearable acoustic acquisition, supporting software, and a clinician-facing review environment. Final specifications, outputs, and user requirements remain under development.

Vest system Multiple acoustic positions, defined processing, and human review.
Investigational
Capture Acquire time-stamped acoustic signals under a defined recording protocol.
Quality control Apply specified checks and processing steps to identify usable and unusable recordings.
Review Present defined recordings and associated information to a qualified human reviewer.

Illustrative development concept. Final channel count and sensor positions require controlled approval.

Heart sounds Multi-point acoustic acquisition is under technical and clinical evaluation.
Lung sounds Proposed pulmonary applications require separately defined evidence and intended use.
Repeat recordings Longitudinal comparison remains a potential future workflow for evaluation.
Proposed Workflow

A proposed workflow from preparation to human review

This preliminary workflow is derived from the development concept. Each step requires controlled specifications, intended-user definition, and human-factors validation.

1

Prepare and fit

Identify the patient and device, apply the appropriate vest or accessory, and confirm placement under a defined protocol.

→
2

Acquire and transfer

Obtain recordings under specified conditions, monitor signal quality, and transfer or store the data using defined controls.

→
3

Qualified human review

Make the defined acoustic information available to the intended reviewer and document follow-up only within the authorized clinical role.

Controlled setupSizing, placement, cleaning, and use-error controls remain to be defined.
Recording qualityAcquisition criteria, thresholds, and failed-recording rules require verification.
Human interpretationReviewer qualifications, report content, and escalation requirements remain under development.
